fields.Front: List the eleven advantages of OOP covered in Week 1.
fields.Back: Modularity, Reusability, Encapsulation, Maintainability, Extensibility, Polymorphism, Inheritance, Team Collaboration, Security and Access Control, Scaling, Debugging and Testing.

fields.Front: Advantage: Modularity. Definition and slide example?
fields.Back: Breaking a system into smaller, manageable pieces, each class self-contained and performing a specific function, making the system easier to understand, develop, and maintain. Example: in an e-commerce system, ShoppingCart, Order, and Payment can be developed independently.

fields.Front: Advantage: Reusability. Definition and slide example?
fields.Back: Code reuse through inheritance and polymorphism: create generalized classes and extend them to handle specific cases with subclasses. Example: a base class Vehicle reused for Car, Bike, and Truck, each reusing the base functionality and extending where needed.

fields.Front: Advantage: Encapsulation. Definition and slide example?
fields.Back: Control over the data, so it is accessed or modified only in an intended way, protecting the object's state from outside interference and reducing bugs and unintended side effects. Example: BankAccount exposes deposit() and withdraw() but keeps balance private.

fields.Front: Advantage: Polymorphism. Definition and slide example?
fields.Back: Objects of different classes can be treated as objects of a common superclass, giving flexibility to operate on objects generically. Example: a PaymentMethod interface with CreditCardPayment, PayPalPayment, and CryptoPayment implementations; new payment types are added without changing the payment-processing logic.

fields.Front: Advantage: Inheritance. Definition and slide example?
fields.Back: Classes inherit properties and methods from other classes, encouraging reuse, reducing duplication, and allowing hierarchical relationships. Example: a game base class Character with health, strength, move(), attack(); Warrior and Mage inherit and add unique abilities.

fields.Front: Advantage: Team Collaboration. Definition and slide example?
fields.Back: Clearly defined interfaces and class responsibilities let different team members work on separate parts of the system. Example: one team develops the User class and its logic while another handles Transaction. Directly relevant to the paired project: agree on class interfaces early.

fields.Front: Advantage: Security and Access Control. Slide example?
fields.Back: Access modifiers restrict access to parts of the system. Example: in a banking application, sensitive operations such as transferring money are handled by a BankTransaction class that limits access to certain methods based on user roles, preventing unauthorized access.

Because OOP isolates parts of the system, individual components can be scaled without affecting others. Example: in a microservices architecture each service (UserService, PaymentService) is an object with a well-defined interface, and PaymentService can be scaled independently for more traffic.

fields.Front: Advantage: Debugging and Testing. Definition and slide example?
fields.Back: Classes are self-contained units that can be tested independently; mock objects or dependency injection let you test a class in isolation. Example: test the Order class by mocking external dependencies like Payment or Shipping.

fields.Front: Which three SOLID principles are name-dropped in Week 1, and what is each attached to?
fields.Back: Single Responsibility Principle (high cohesion), Dependency Inversion Principle (low coupling), Open/Closed Principle (extensibility). All three are covered fully in later lectures.

fields.Text: Maintainability in OOP rests on {{c1::separation of concerns}}: a bug in the `{{c1::Payment}} class of an online store can be fixed without affecting ShoppingCart or Order`.
fields.Extra: Each class is responsible for a specific part of the system, so changes are often isolated to a single class.

fields.Text: Extensibility means code is open for {{c1::extension}} but closed for {{c1::modification}}, which is the {{c1::Open/Closed Principle}}.
fields.Extra: You extend functionality by adding new classes or methods without changing existing code. Adding Triangle to the Shape hierarchy is the canonical illustration.

fields.Text: The eleven OOP advantages: modularity, reusability, {{c1::encapsulation}}, maintainability, {{c1::extensibility}}, polymorphism, inheritance, {{c1::team collaboration}}, security and access control, {{c1::scaling}}, and debugging and testing.

Advantage examples: modularity - {{c1::ShoppingCart, Order, Payment}} developed independently; reusability - base class {{c1::Vehicle}} reused for Car, Bike, Truck; inheritance - game base class {{c1::Character}} extended by Warrior and Mage.
Testing is easier in OOP because classes are {{c1::self-contained units}} testable independently, using {{c1::mock objects or dependency injection}}; e.g. test Order by mocking Payment and Shipping.
Scaling example: in a {{c1::microservices}} architecture each service (UserService, PaymentService) is an object with a well-defined interface, so PaymentService can be {{c1::scaled independently}}.
